newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: YEAREND - Asia refiners face uncertain 1997.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Asia refiners face uncertain 1997.

text.p: Asian oil refiners had mixed fortunes in 1996 and next year's prospects hinge on how well they cut costs and adapt to rising global competition as domestic oil industries deregulate, industry sources said.

Singapore refineries did better this year compared to 1995, but those in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan suffered from a combination of factors -- high crude and low retail product prices, currency depreciation and oil sector liberalisation.
"With deregulation, Japan, South Korea, the Philippines, and Thailand now have to compete in a free market," a Singapore refiner said. "This means only the fittest will survive."

He said Japanese and South Korean refiners have to be more efficient in running their plants, while the mature refineries in Singapore are better geared for a free market as they have been export-oriented from the outset.
Industry sources said refineries could perform well in 1997 -- if they succeed in raising domestic prices, operate efficiently and cut refinery runs promptly when profit margins are low.
Refiners also need to learn to hedge crude purchases more efficiently by using sophisticated derivative tools in a volatile market, analysts said.
SOME YEARS OF UNCERTAINTY

However, Singapore refiners said prospects for 1997 appeared mixed. Refining capacity rose in 1996 to an estimated 17.9 million barrels per day (bpd), as an extra 1.43 million bpd of capacity came onstream in the last year or so.

"Short of any major unforeseen disruptions, there will be continuing downward pressure on refinery margins in general, because of additional refining capacity which has come onstream in 1996," Shell Singapore said in a statement in response to questions from Reuters.

But Mobil Oil Singapore, a unit of U.S. oil giant Mobil Corp, said: "Winter in the U.S., Europe and China, coinciding with low inventory levels are likely to sustain reasonable margins through the first quarter of 1997."
Mobil said the fundamentals for crude supply were stable. "Volatility in pricing is generally short term and news-driven and therefore hard to predict," a company spokesman said.
Refiners estimated 1996/1997 demand growth for products at four percent against average Asia Pacific consumption of more than 18 million bpd in 1996.
"Over the longer term, regional demand will continue to be healthy but we foresee that it would probably take around three years for regional demand to outpace supply," Mobil said.

Asian refiners saw volatile basic refining margins in 1996, ranging from $4.00 per barrel profit to a 50-cent loss, along with higher average benchmark Brent crude price of $17 a barrel, over initial projections of $15-$16, analysts said.
Average Brent prices in 1997 are projected at $19-$20, said Tom James, Asia Pacific regional manager for Natural Resources at Credit Lyonnais Rouse Derivatives.
JAPAN LOOKS TO RETAIL MARKET
Nevertheless, refiners in Singapore surveyed by Reuters said profit margins this year had been better than expected due to five-year high prices for diesel and jet/kerosene.
"Margins have been positive in the last quarter and over the course of the year have been better than expected, being positive for eight out of 12 months," a Mobil spokesman said.
One refiner said profitability for regional refineries was also boosted by a lack of imports from outside Asia, unlike in recent years.
But for Japanese refiners, who sell mostly to the domestic market, margins were squeezed by poor retail product prices.

"Judging from company results, margins have deteriorated this year from last year," an industry official said. "Oil firms are making various efforts to cuts costs, such as in distribution, so they can survive with low margins."
Japan's 10 major leading firms saw a sharp 57.4-percent fall in current profits to a combined 17.7 billion yen in the six months to September, the Petroleum Association of Japan said.

In April, Japan liberalised oil product imports, previously dominated by local oil firms. To combat imports, big refiners introduced a new wholesale pricing system which cut the price of gasoline while raising diesel and kerosene.
Margins next year will depend on whether or not the retail market recovers, Japanese oil industry sources said.
In a bid to tighten supplies and boost diesel and kerosene prices, oil firms have been keeping refinery operating rates at low levels this year.
"Refiners are expected to keep refinery runs low next year to try to boost kerosene and gas oil (diesel) retail prices," said Masaru Ohkawa, analyst with Nomura Research Institute Ltd.
"Higher costs from low refinery runs have had a damaging effect on profits, but oil firms are making various efforts to cut costs in other areas," he said.
SOUTH KOREA FREES PRICE CONTROLS
South Korean oil firms are expected to post a huge loss in the refining sector this year, plagued by the won's sharp fall against the dollar.
Analysts said the estimated aggregate net loss for Korea's five refiners would widen to around 350 billion won ($422 million), against a 8.45-billion-won shortfall last year.

Refiners' foreign exchange loss would account for almost 70 percent of net losses. "Refiners carry a lot of dollar-denominated debt, and the won has depreciated seven percent against the dollar so far this year," said George Goundry, an energy analyst with HG Asia.

But analysts said prospects are better next year with a more stable won and price liberalisation on January 1. "Refiners will try to raise product prices when they are deregulated," said Yong Han, oil analyst at Jardine Fleming Securities.

Removal of fixed prices will lift curbs on refinery profits. "Stable dollar/won rate, low crude prices and deregulation could improve business result for oil refiners next year," said Goundry. "It has a potential to look better than this year."
